lesson.menu_title: The Weight of Words — Official Language Decoded
lesson.menu_desc: A communique of two hundred words, and everything it was written not to say -- 37 slides
lesson.subtitle: Lesson 6 -- The Weight of Words
lesson.title_tag: Professor View -- Henrique Monteiro Neto | Lesson 6 -- The Weight of Words

listenings.text: Following the conclusion of this week's meetings, the parties reaffirm their commitment to the principles set out in the framework agreement. A comprehensive review of implementation has taken place, and there has been a marked improvement in cooperation since January. The parties take note of the report submitted by the smaller delegations and welcome its contribution to the discussion. An undertaking has been given with respect to the transfer of resources, subject to a further review, the timing of which will be determined in due course. The parties look forward to continued engagement in a spirit of good faith. That is the full text of the statement. There will be no questions this evening.

Off the record? We agreed the policy on the first afternoon. Everything after that was wording. Four days, and at the end of it we were stuck on one adverb, and three capitals had to approve the change. People laugh when I tell them that, and they should not, because the adverb decided whether the obligation had a date attached to it. Ambiguity gets a terrible press, and sometimes it is the only text everybody can sign, and a text everybody signs is worth more than a perfect text nobody signs. What I do regret is paragraph six. We gave an undertaking with no date, and I wrote part of it, and I knew at the time what we were doing. That one I would take back.

extra_audio.text: Ingrid says her job is closer to demolition than to translation. He asks who decides what changes when a sentence does not survive. She explains that she says what breaks and the delegations decide what to do about it. He asks whether the ambiguity is ever deliberate. She answers that it frequently is, and that the loophole nobody noticed is the real problem.

paras: The communique is two hundred words long and it took four days to write. That is not incompetence. The policy had been agreed in the first afternoon; what remained was the wording, and the wording is where the argument actually lives.

Read the verbs, or rather notice how few there are. The parties "reaffirm their commitment" to a principle that nobody in the room had questioned, which tells you the principle was never at issue. They "take note of" the report from the smaller states — a phrase which acknowledges that the report exists and commits the reader to precisely nothing further. And there has been, we are told, "a marked improvement in cooperation", a sentence in which cooperation improves all by itself and nobody is thanked or blamed.

Paragraph six is the one to read twice. It contains an undertaking, which is real, and a deadline, which is subject to a review that has not been scheduled. It is not binding, and every delegation signing it knew that. The text had been watered down twice by Wednesday, and by Thursday the talks were in deadlock over a single adverb, which three capitals eventually had to sign off on.

What broke it was a face-saving formula about timing: the obligation stands, the date does not. The result falls short of what the smaller states asked for, and is couched in language warm enough that they can present it at home as progress. Whether that is diplomacy working or diplomacy failing is a genuine question, and the answer depends on what you think two hundred words are for.

gist.prompt: What is this analysis mainly about?
choices: Why the meeting failed to reach any agreement at all
How the wording of an official text decides what it actually obliges anybody to do
Why communiques should be written in plain language
